thread.title: Staying Out Of The Market's Rush

author: The Idea Guide
title: Staying Out Of The Market's Rush
text:
by Daniel Shvartsman
Markets are getting wild again - we're up 3.3% as I write this on news Jerome Powell may be backing away from hikes - and my brief observation is that a lot of investors are turning into sports fans, cheering or booing results rather than studying them. One way to back away from that is to dig into individual ideas that aren't necessarily subject to the market's whims, and that's what I target on today's Idea Guide.
Short Ideas We published 28 short ideas over the past two weeks. Tesla ( TSLA ) continues to predominate with six short ideas, and there are three pot-related ideas. Here are five other ideas to check out.
Time To Short Catastrophe Reinsurer, Blue Capital Reinsurance by Saidrasul Nasretdinov
Blue Capital Reinsurance ( BCRH ) is 33% owned by Endurance Holdings ( ENH ), which is no longer publicly traded but instead owned by Sompo ( OTCPK:SMPNY ). ENH came into that ownership through acquiring Montpelier RE. BCRH is based in Bermuda.
So far, fairly mundane in the insurance world. I remember studying BCRH for a while not long after it came public, since it screened cheaply (below tangible book value), and not understanding the Montpelier angle or why that would ever benefit BCRH shareholders.
Saidrasul Nasretdinov argues now is the time to short BCRH, which is interesting based on this chart:
That doesn't mean it's wrong! His argument centers on the likelihood BCRH - based on past habits - has underestimated the losses it will have to take related to its insurance business, faces a tough pricing environment for reinsurance, and doesn't get much benefit from interest rates. The company trades at half of its tangible book value (though a slightly higher multiple when you factor in the company's reported Q4 losses ), so the math game becomes 'how much of this is the market pricing in already, and the technical dynamics as it would seem a lot of people have benefited from BCRH's sell-off over the past year. The company still portends to pay a $.30 quarterly dividend, which as you can see in the image means a nearly 20% yield.
Sentiment - The CrickAnt has covered the company regularly and turned bearish on it last summer. Comments here were mixed, though some questions about the wisdom of shorting a company trading at such a discount, or the risk that Sompo might step in.
OneSpan: Plagued By Anemic Growth by Skyward Investments OneSpan ( OSPN ) is VASCO Data Security's ( VDSI-OLD ) new name (see this news ). VDSI used to be a bit of a battleground, with skeptics pointing to the company's hardware dependent obsolescence - anecdote is that in various European countries, my wife and I used to use VDSI type signature keys, but now do everything through our phones - while bulls pointing to the solid balance sheet and cash flow.
Skyward Investments has written about OneSpan a couple of times - the first person to write about it or VDSI since 2016. This article sticks closely to the financials, highlighting the price paid for Dealflo and the slow revenue growth despite this (the 10Q reports $1.8M in revenue from Dealflo in Q3, as compared to $52.5M in total revenue). There's no smoking gun sort of thesis here, but it does highlight some concerns for the company - burning cash, even though there's a decent buffer, and slim revenue growth and earnings - that may make it interesting to revisit as a short.
Sentiment - While VDSI was a battleground, OSPN hasn't attracted much attention at all. A couple comments on Skyward's previous article were mildly more bullish.
Digimarc: Good Short Opportunity by Timid Capital Timid Capital is new to SA, and unwittingly shook a hornets' nest in calling Digimarc ( DMRC ) a short. The company provides watermarking and tools that prevent piracy, counterfeit behavior, and other fraud in the market. The author looks at declining revenues, regular equity issuance, and increasing SG&A spending and deduces that the picture is not great, especially when the company's core business doesn't seem to have an obvious moat.
Not so fast, say our commenters. They point to a currencies business that is worth the value of the shares alone, leaving optionality around the watermarking/retail business, with just one big contract enough to break the news.
There's a good back and forth, including one bear and mostly bulls, in the comment stream. It reminds me of the last DMRC article I read on SA, which dates back to nearly three years ago. The author said earnings were unlikely until 2018 at the earliest, that revenue might be $30M in 2018, and that the shares should trade in mid teens. The comment stream there disagreed with the author sharply, but as of Q3 2018, TTM revenue is $21M and the other realities have played out.
Sentiment - As mentioned, mostly bullish in the comments. We haven't had an article since 2017, though the coverage has leaned more bullish than negative.
We Believe Novavax's RSV F Vaccine Is Likely To Fail Again And That Novavax Is Hurtling Toward Insolvency by Alpha Exposure Biotech ideas can get obscured quickly by jargon and shrouded targets, and Alpha Exposure avoids that by laying out the issue for Novavax ( NVAX ) in the introduction. The company is aiming to produce a lifelong vaccine for RSV, but the virus changes or mutates over time, so that a lifelong vaccine isn't practical. That would make the challenge of passing the company's Phase 3 trial more difficult. Failure leaves the company with a levered balance sheet and not much hope of continuing to develop equity value (though they just announced a cash raise after the article).
That's basically the argument. It appears to be well supported - though fiercely contested, as per below - and we should have results from the trial this quarter, so there will be a near-term resolution to this specific question.
Sentiment - Comments are bullish with more than a bit of anger that a shortseller would write up the stock (not a bullish sign, generally). Most articles are bullish about the company, and six different authors wrote it up positively in 2018.
Deere: Material Downside Into 2019 by Michael Boyd Deere ( DE ) and Caterpillar ( CAT ) are cyclical companies that have had targets on their backs from shortsellers for a few years, but have mostly defied the skeptics. Both have pulled back in the last year, Caterpillar more so, but they haven't been great shorts yet. Michael Boyd makes the case that this will change for Deere.
He revisits a pillar of past short theses (for example ) which is that Deere has defied the cycle due to financing of new sales, something that can't last forever. As farmland value remains pressured, this makes it tough for Deere to maintain margins or engineer growth. It's a compelling thesis, but I also thought that back in 2014.
Sentiment Check - Comments go back and forth between approval of the analysis and a bit of reflexive dismissal and faith in DE's management. While the previous article on Deere was also bearish, most other coverage in 2018 was bullish.
Long Ideas We published 346 long ideas in the past two weeks. GE and Apple ( AAPL ) remain top topics - Apple makes up seven of our most read 20 long ideas, and GE makes up another four. Here are a few less followed stories:
The Case For Why Freeport-McMoRan Is Almost Criminally Undervalued by Robert Kientz Freeport-McMoRan ( FCX ) is trading near 2-year lows , and is a commodity producer. Those would appear to be related, especially as copper (FCX's key commodity) bounced off 18-month lows only this week . Kientz argues that copper pricing will have to go higher due to supply shortfalls, including a Freeport mine in 2019, and that the company has done yeoman's work in cutting down debt - indeed, it's down to $6.6B, compared to $10B in equity. He also spends time on the recent issue over a mine in Indonesia that appears to have weighed on shares. For a long position at this point, it would help to see how the company does in a prolonged copper trough or a global recession, and whether it comes out the other side ok. As long as there's a case to be made that FCX can grind through that, there does seem to be an upside story as Kientz points out.
Sentiment Check - The last five authors who have covered FCX are bullish or very bullish on the stock. Comments are fairly bullish, though a few people pointed out that there's nothing to stop FCX from going lower.
Lending Club: $1.15 Billion Market Cap, $800 Million In Cash by Billy Duberstein Billy Duberstein presents Lending Club ( LC ) as more of a two-sided internet platform than a bank. The company brings savers and borrowers together but with less of a middleman than a traditional bank. That poses an interesting challenge in terms of valuing the company. Duberstein takes the adjusted earnings numbers and argues you can net out the cash from the balance sheet and consider an EV/Sales and EV/EBITDA. Even on a P/TBV basis, the stock is at 1.36x, which isn't great but isn't too high either. The question is whether those are the right ways to think about the business.
Sentiment Check - Comments are bullish except for commenters who have participated in Lending Club as lenders (if I understood correctly). 3 of the most recent 4 authors on the stock are bullish.
Colony Credit: Satisfactory Progress And Bargain Valuation by John Sheehy Staying in finance, we move to Colony Credit ( CLNC ), a mortgage REIT. John Sheehy writes up the company as trading at an outlier valuation (on a book value basis) and growing its core earnings. The issue with Colony is its association with Colony Capital ( CLNY ) and the NorthStar compound, which has had poor returns over recent years. Mortgage REITs are often math problems to be solved, but the variable of management issues is harder to tackle.
Sentiment Check - Comments reflect disgust with management. Sheehy has been the main analyst on CLNC, though the one other article we posted in 2018 was neutral to bearish.
Obalon Therapeutics: Playing The Aesthetics Business by Trading Places Research Obalon ( OBLN ) makes gas-filled balloons that are put in a pill, ingested, and then inflate in a patient's stomach to make them less hungry. So it's sort of a plastic surgery/aesthetics play without as much surgery. It sounds sort of science fiction, but the company received a recent FDA approval and is beginning to pursue a plan to bring this to market. Trading Places Research spells out this speculation - which they are waiting on given overall market conditions - and it's of interest to me not as an investment, but for the concept that there are some segments of the market that just don't seem to be winners. Antibiotics is one that I've discussed in the Idea Guide, and aesthetics seems to be another - Cutera ( CTRA ) hasn't done well, Sientra ( SIEN ) has been up and down at best, and a few other names are echoing in my head but I can't quite recall them. It's unclear to me what the common thread is, because it would seem like there is demand for these sorts of products, even if they operate in less clear medical spaces.
Sentiment Check - No coverage since IPO in 2016, and the comments appeared to draw out a couple investors who are following this very closely.
Laura Ashley: Low Downside Risk, Great Upside by Dimitrios Koutsoubos Laura Ashley ( OTC:LARAF ) is a micro-cap and a very small one (trades as ALY.L in London), but it caught my eye since I see their stores occasionally in Europe, so the micro-cap status surprised me. Koutsoubos gives a full history of the British brand, which now has majority shareholders from Japan and Malaysia (controlling a combined 61% of the company). The company has fallen back into turnaround status, and there are a few quirks here - the company sold off real estate in Singapore, it has £250M in revenue and franchising means the actual brand sales are higher, and there are doubts in management. But it's an interesting story, and for enterprising investors may be worth researching.
Sentiment Check - The comments are positive and bring out a few Europeans with more direct experience with LARAF.
***
That's it for this week's Idea Guide. This newsletter provides a weekly review of our long and short ideas that comes out on Fridays, exclusively for SA Essential and PRO+ subscribers. If you have feedback, email me at daniel@seekingalpha.com . We're looking to continue to make the website more useful for readers, so your feedback will be invaluable. Follow the account if you'd like to get this in your inbox.
Wishing you a successful 2019 and the ability to ride out the ups and downs of the market while still sleeping and meeting your investment goals!
Disclosure: I/we have no positions in any stocks mentioned, and no plans to initiate any positions within the next 72 hours. I wrote this article myself, and it expresses my own opinions.
